The papersThe code

Class imbalance, dug back up.

Blagus and Lusa ran their simulations and the breast cancer analysis in R and published them in 2010 without the code. In November 2026 we rebuilt both from the paper (an R package, multds, with the nine classifiers, the three corrections and the measures) and reran the settings the figures and tables need, except MultDS for RF, SVM and PAM (and, with centred variables, for six classifiers), which our compute budget left out. Of 50 results, 16 are exact, 9 agree, 21 partly agree, 1 differ and 3 were not attempted. Every gap has a cause; 18 stay open, chiefly the SVM's and PAM's unstated settings, the sample centring of the p = 40 panels, RF-THR in the null case and the tails of a few prediction intervals.

Fig. 1

Fig. 1. Null case, p = 40, no selection: PA (filled), PA1 and PA2 (open) against k1train; test set as imbalanced as the training set.

Partly agrees
Fig. 1: null case, p = 40, no selection; PA, PA1, PA2 against k1train (nine classifiers)
473 of 513 values within tolerance, Partly agrees

(1) SVM: the paper gives no cost, and its class weights ('the proportion of samples from each class') leave the direction open. With the default cost 1 our SVM is less biased than the paper's in the simulations (Additional file 3, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.18 against 0.03; there the weights change nothing at cost 1). A smaller cost with the stated weights brings Additional file 3 back (cost 0.1: 0.08; 0.03: 0.00) but sends the null case of Fig. 2 to 0 (cost 0.1: 0.001 against 0.038). On the breast cancer data the stated weights go the wrong way (20 ER+ / 5 ER-, PA ER-: 0.46 at cost 1 against 0.6); weights inverse to the class sizes with cost 0.1 give 0.60 there but 0.56 at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (paper 0.49). Weights taken from the original rather than the over-sampled training set change nothing (Additional file 8, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.22 and 0.22). No cost and weighting of the grid fits all of them. (2) PAM without correction: our PAM is slightly more biased than the paper's near balance in the null case (Fig. 1, k1train 0.45: PA1 0.23 against 0.27) and at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (PA ER- 0.47 against 0.53). The paper says the threshold was the one with the smallest training error, not which one of the ties. The smallest tied threshold gives 0.24 and 0.47; 10-fold CV 0.09 and 0.56; equal class priors 0.46 and 0.63. None fits both. Without variable selection (Additional file 6) the difference runs the other way: the paper's PAM puts nearly every sample in the majority class (k1train 0.2: PA 0.52), ours less so (0.73). (3) Values near 0 or 1: a few points where our replicates are all or nearly all 0 or 1, so the Monte Carlo tolerance is close to 0, and the paper's values differ from ours by less than 0.003.

Fig. 3

Fig. 3. Alternative case, mu2 = 1: PA1 with 20 (left) or all (right) variables differing.

Partly agrees
Fig. 3: alternative case, pDE = 20 or p, G = 40; PA1 (1-NN, DLDA, PLR)
121 of 270 values within tolerance, Partly agrees

p = 40 and pDE = p: the paper says the samples were centred, and with centring our minority-class PA is far below the paper's where 20 of 40 or all of the variables differ (9 of 156 such points of Fig. 3 match, 32 of 171 of Additional file 4, 27 of 297 of Additional file 5). Centring the samples over 40 variables of which half or all are shifted removes most of the signal. Rerunning these settings without centring (200 replicates) matches 155 of 156 points of Fig. 3, 112 of 171 of Additional file 4 and 254 of 297 of Additional file 5; what still misses is the SVM, PAM at pDE = p, and the k1train = 0.95 end at pDE = 20, where the paper's PA1 is a little lower than either of our runs. Our run keeps the stated centring.

Partly agrees
Fig. 5: no correction, over-sampling, down-sizing, MultDS; PA, PA1, PA2 (3-NN, DLDA, PLR)
625 of 684 values within tolerance, Partly agrees

(1) Over-sampling, overall PA: Fig. 5's over-sampling PA is the PA of a test set as imbalanced as the training set (k1 PA1 + (1 - k1) PA2 from our class-specific means: 50 of 57 points match, against 19 for the balanced test set the caption implies), while Additional file 8, which repeats the panel for all classifiers, uses the balanced test set (109 of 171 against 59). The two figures disagree; we compare with the balanced test set. (2) Over-sampling, order of selection: with variables selected on the original training set and the classifier fitted on the over-sampled one, DLDA's and DQDA's PA at k1train 0.2 is 0.88 and 0.79 (paper: 0.88, 0.79); selecting on the over-sampled set, which the Methods describe and our run does, gives 0.85 and 0.74. The k-NN classifiers move little either way (3-NN 0.86 / 0.85). (3) Values near 0 or 1: a few points where our replicates are all or nearly all 0 or 1, so the Monte Carlo tolerance is close to 0, and the paper's values differ from ours by less than 0.003.

192 of 192 values within tolerance, Agrees
Fig. 6: 95% prediction intervals of the class-specific PA
377 of 382 values within tolerance, Partly agrees

Prediction intervals: a few interval ends miss by two steps of 0.05, nearly all lower ends at the smallest training sets (377 of 382 ends of Fig. 6 and 930 of 976 of Additional file 12 match). The lower 2.5th percentile of 500 draws rests on its 13 lowest values, which the paper's draws (unknown seeds) and ours place differently. Other interval definitions fit worse: mean -/+ 1.96 SD matches 310 and 703, 5th and 95th percentiles 361 and 893.

Additional file 8: Fig. 5 for all nine classifiers (MultDS for six)
1655 of 1881 values within tolerance, Partly agrees

(1) SVM: the paper gives no cost, and its class weights ('the proportion of samples from each class') leave the direction open. With the default cost 1 our SVM is less biased than the paper's in the simulations (Additional file 3, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.18 against 0.03; there the weights change nothing at cost 1). A smaller cost with the stated weights brings Additional file 3 back (cost 0.1: 0.08; 0.03: 0.00) but sends the null case of Fig. 2 to 0 (cost 0.1: 0.001 against 0.038). On the breast cancer data the stated weights go the wrong way (20 ER+ / 5 ER-, PA ER-: 0.46 at cost 1 against 0.6); weights inverse to the class sizes with cost 0.1 give 0.60 there but 0.56 at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (paper 0.49). Weights taken from the original rather than the over-sampled training set change nothing (Additional file 8, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.22 and 0.22). No cost and weighting of the grid fits all of them. (2) PAM with over-sampling: the paper's PAM stays fully biased after over-sampling (Additional file 8, k1train 0.1: PA 0.51; Additional file 9, k1train 0.05: PA1 0.02), ours does not (0.75, 0.74): pamr's class prior defaults to the class shares of the set it is trained on, which over-sampling makes equal. Keeping the prior of the original training set gives 0.51 and 0.06. The k-NN classifiers move little either way (3-NN 0.86 / 0.85). (4) Over-sampling, overall PA: Fig. 5's over-sampling PA is the PA of a test set as imbalanced as the training set (k1 PA1 + (1 - k1) PA2 from our class-specific means: 50 of 57 points match, against 19 for the balanced test set the caption implies), while Additional file 8, which repeats the panel for all classifiers, uses the balanced test set (109 of 171 against 59). The two figures disagree; we compare with the balanced test set.

(1) SVM: the paper gives no cost, and its class weights ('the proportion of samples from each class') leave the direction open. With the default cost 1 our SVM is less biased than the paper's in the simulations (Additional file 3, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.18 against 0.03; there the weights change nothing at cost 1). A smaller cost with the stated weights brings Additional file 3 back (cost 0.1: 0.08; 0.03: 0.00) but sends the null case of Fig. 2 to 0 (cost 0.1: 0.001 against 0.038). On the breast cancer data the stated weights go the wrong way (20 ER+ / 5 ER-, PA ER-: 0.46 at cost 1 against 0.6); weights inverse to the class sizes with cost 0.1 give 0.60 there but 0.56 at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (paper 0.49). Weights taken from the original rather than the over-sampled training set change nothing (Additional file 8, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.22 and 0.22). No cost and weighting of the grid fits all of them. (2) DQDA's AUC: lower than the paper's when the training set is imbalanced (k1train 0.1: 0.87 against 0.91). The paper does not say which score it ranked. Ranking by the ratio of the two discriminants instead of their difference gives the paper's AUC at every k1train (0.91, 0.98, 0.99, 0.99, 0.99) and moves DLDA's AUC only from 0.94 to 0.95 at 0.1 (paper 0.94); the predictions do not change. Found by search over five scores; our run keeps the difference.

(1) SVM: the paper gives no cost, and its class weights ('the proportion of samples from each class') leave the direction open. With the default cost 1 our SVM is less biased than the paper's in the simulations (Additional file 3, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.18 against 0.03; there the weights change nothing at cost 1). A smaller cost with the stated weights brings Additional file 3 back (cost 0.1: 0.08; 0.03: 0.00) but sends the null case of Fig. 2 to 0 (cost 0.1: 0.001 against 0.038). On the breast cancer data the stated weights go the wrong way (20 ER+ / 5 ER-, PA ER-: 0.46 at cost 1 against 0.6); weights inverse to the class sizes with cost 0.1 give 0.60 there but 0.56 at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (paper 0.49). Weights taken from the original rather than the over-sampled training set change nothing (Additional file 8, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.22 and 0.22). No cost and weighting of the grid fits all of them. (2) PAM without correction: our PAM is slightly more biased than the paper's near balance in the null case (Fig. 1, k1train 0.45: PA1 0.23 against 0.27) and at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (PA ER- 0.47 against 0.53). The paper says the threshold was the one with the smallest training error, not which one of the ties. The smallest tied threshold gives 0.24 and 0.47; 10-fold CV 0.09 and 0.56; equal class priors 0.46 and 0.63. None fits both. Without variable selection (Additional file 6) the difference runs the other way: the paper's PAM puts nearly every sample in the majority class (k1train 0.2: PA 0.52), ours less so (0.73).

SVM: the paper gives no cost, and its class weights ('the proportion of samples from each class') leave the direction open. With the default cost 1 our SVM is less biased than the paper's in the simulations (Additional file 3, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.18 against 0.03; there the weights change nothing at cost 1). A smaller cost with the stated weights brings Additional file 3 back (cost 0.1: 0.08; 0.03: 0.00) but sends the null case of Fig. 2 to 0 (cost 0.1: 0.001 against 0.038). On the breast cancer data the stated weights go the wrong way (20 ER+ / 5 ER-, PA ER-: 0.46 at cost 1 against 0.6); weights inverse to the class sizes with cost 0.1 give 0.60 there but 0.56 at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (paper 0.49). Weights taken from the original rather than the over-sampled training set change nothing (Additional file 8, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.22 and 0.22). No cost and weighting of the grid fits all of them.

Each result of the paper, with the verdict computed from results.json and, for each one that is not exact, why.

Fig. 1: null case, p = 40, no selection; PA, PA1, PA2 against k1train (nine classifiers)Partly agrees473 of 513 values within tolerance(1) SVM: the paper gives no cost, and its class weights ('the proportion of samples from each class') leave the direction open. A smaller cost with the stated weights brings Additional file 3 back (cost 0.1: 0.08; 0.03: 0.00) but sends the null case of Fig. 2 to 0 (cost 0.1: 0.001 against 0.038). On the breast cancer data the stated weights go the wrong way (20 ER+ / 5 ER-, PA ER-: 0.46 at cost 1 against 0.6); weights inverse to the class sizes with cost 0.1 give 0.60 there but 0.56 at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (paper 0.49). Weights taken from the original rather than the over-sampled training set change nothing (Additional file 8, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.22 and 0.22). No cost and weighting of the grid fits all of them. (2) PAM without correction: our PAM is slightly more biased than the paper's near balance in the null case (Fig. 1, k1train 0.45: PA1 0.23 against 0.27) and at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (PA ER- 0.47 against 0.53). The paper says the threshold was the one with the smallest training error, not which one of the ties. Fig. 3: alternative case, pDE = 20 or p, G = 40; PA1 (1-NN, DLDA, PLR)Partly agrees121 of 270 values within tolerancep = 40 and pDE = p: the paper says the samples were centred, and with centring our minority-class PA is far below the paper's where 20 of 40 or all of the variables differ (9 of 156 such points of Fig. 3 match, 32 of 171 of Additional file 4, 27 of 297 of Additional file 5). Centring the samples over 40 variables of which half or all are shifted removes most of the signal. Rerunning these settings without centring (200 replicates) matches 155 of 156 points of Fig. 3, 112 of 171 of Additional file 4 and 254 of 297 of Additional file 5; what still misses is the SVM, PAM at pDE = p, and the k1train = 0.95 end at pDE = 20, where the paper's PA1 is a little lower than either of our runs. Our run keeps the stated centring.

Fig. 5: no correction, over-sampling, down-sizing, MultDS; PA, PA1, PA2 (3-NN, DLDA, PLR)Partly agrees625 of 684 values within tolerance(1) Over-sampling, overall PA: Fig. 5's over-sampling PA is the PA of a test set as imbalanced as the training set (k1 PA1 + (1 - k1) PA2 from our class-specific means: 50 of 57 points match, against 19 for the balanced test set the caption implies), while Additional file 8, which repeats the panel for all classifiers, uses the balanced test set (109 of 171 against 59). The two figures disagree; we compare with the balanced test set. (2) Over-sampling, order of selection: with variables selected on the original training set and the classifier fitted on the over-sampled one, DLDA's and DQDA's PA at k1train 0.2 is 0.88 and 0.79 (paper: 0.88, 0.79); selecting on the over-sampled set, which the Methods describe and our run does, gives 0.85 and 0.74. The k-NN classifiers move little either way (3-NN 0.86 / 0.85). (3) Values near 0 or 1: a few points where our replicates are all or nearly all 0 or 1, so the Monte Carlo tolerance is close to 0, and the paper's values differ from ours by less than 0.003.

(4) Over-sampling, overall PA: Fig. 5's over-sampling PA is the PA of a test set as imbalanced as the training set (k1 PA1 + (1 - k1) PA2 from our class-specific means: 50 of 57 points match, against 19 for the balanced test set the caption implies), while Additional file 8, which repeats the panel for all classifiers, uses the balanced test set (109 of 171 against 59). (1) SVM: the paper gives no cost, and its class weights ('the proportion of samples from each class') leave the direction open. With the default cost 1 our SVM is less biased than the paper's in the simulations (Additional file 3, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.18 against 0.03; there the weights change nothing at cost 1). A smaller cost with the stated weights brings Additional file 3 back (cost 0.1: 0.08; 0.03: 0.00) but sends the null case of Fig. 2 to 0 (cost 0.1: 0.001 against 0.038). On the breast cancer data the stated weights go the wrong way (20 ER+ / 5 ER-, PA ER-: 0.46 at cost 1 against 0.6); weights inverse to the class sizes with cost 0.1 give 0.60 there but 0.56 at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (paper 0.49). Weights taken from the original rather than the over-sampled training set change nothing (Additional file 8, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.22 and 0.22). No cost and weighting of the grid fits all of them. (2) PAM without correction: our PAM is slightly more biased than the paper's near balance in the null case (Fig. 1, k1train 0.45: PA1 0.23 against 0.27) and at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (PA ER- 0.47 against 0.53). The paper says the threshold was the one with the smallest training error, not which one of the ties. The smallest tied threshold gives 0.24 and 0.47; 10-fold CV 0.09 and 0.56; equal class priors 0.46 and 0.63. None fits both. Without variable selection (Additional file 6) the difference runs the other way: the paper's PAM puts nearly every sample in the majority class (k1train 0.2: PA 0.52), ours less so (0.73).

The main conclusions hold in our run: the classifiers are biased towards the majority class, variable selection adds to the bias, over-sampling helps little for most classifiers, and down-sizing and above all multiple down-sizing remove most of the bias, on the simulations and the breast cancer data. The claims that miss come from the SVM, PAM after over-sampling, RF-THR in the null case, selection at k1train 0.9 and a few interval ends.

What came back

The null case
Figs 1 and 2: every classifier except the SVM and, near balance, PAM came back within Monte Carlo error at p = 40, 1000 and 10000 (473 of 513 and 469 of 513 points).
The corrections
Down-sizing and MultDS (Fig. 5, Additional files 8 and 10) came back point by point for every classifier we ran except the SVM; Additional file 10's intervals match a 20-sample test set (554 of 554 ends), not the 500 its caption says.
The thresholds
RF-THR and PLR-THR (Additional file 11): 114 of 114 points.
The breast cancer data
The Sotiriou arrays came back from the NCI archive: 99 tumours, 7650 probes, 34 ER- and 65 ER+. Fig. 6 came back 192 of 192 means; Additional file 14 (MultDS) 374 of 378 cells.
The code the paper used
DLDA and DQDA are sma's stat.diag.da; our versions give identical predictions, and our AUC equals Hmisc's.

What stayed buried

  • The R scripts. The paper names the packages and released no code; no copy was found.
  • The SVM's cost and the direction of its class weights. No single setting fits the simulations and the breast cancer tables at once.
  • PAM's tie rule for the threshold. Our PAM is a little more biased near balance and at 45 ER+ / 5 ER-; neither the smallest tied threshold, cross-validation nor equal priors fits both.
  • The seeds. A few prediction-interval ends, set by the 13 lowest of 500 draws, land two steps of 0.05 from the paper's.

The main conclusions hold in our run: the classifiers are biased towards the majority class, variable selection adds to the bias, over-sampling helps little for most classifiers, and down-sizing and above all multiple down-sizing remove most of the bias, on the simulations and the breast cancer data. The claims that miss come from the SVM, PAM after over-sampling, RF-THR in the null case, selection at k1train 0.9 and a few interval ends.

What we matched

What the paper does not say, what it says that its figures contradict, and what we chose. Each was tested against the paper's own values.

Sample centring
Stated for every setting, but Fig. 3's p = 40 and pDE = p points come back almost all without it (see the cause of Fig. 3); Additional files 4 and 5 fit much better without it too, though not fully.
Over-sampling
The paper's DLDA and DQDA are fitted better by selection on the original training set, and its PAM by keeping the original class prior after over-sampling (tested at one or two k1train values, 200 replicates). Our run follows the Methods (selection on the over-sampled set, pamr's default prior).
Fig. 5's test set
Its over-sampling PA is that of a test set as imbalanced as the training set; Additional file 8, the same panel for all nine classifiers, uses a balanced one.
DQDA's AUC
Ranked by the ratio of the two discriminants, not their difference: found by search; the predictions are the same.
Additional file 1
Prints PLR's PA1, PA2 and PV1 for all nine classifiers; those cells are listed as paper slips and the rest compared.
Tolerance
The printed precision plus a Bonferroni multiple of the combined Monte Carlo standard error: our SD over our replicate count, plus the paper's SD (ours where it prints none) over the paper's replicate count.

Blagus and Lusa, 2010. The simulations and the breast cancer analysis came back in November 2026, from the paper alone.
